title: 15 A single-pole thermal-magnetic circuit breaker on a base

sources.citation: The 15 A single-pole thermal-magnetic molded-case breaker of NEC-region branch circuits, listed to UL 489. Paraphrased, not reproduced: it carries its rating continuously, and must trip within an hour at 135 % (for ratings up to 50 A) and within two minutes at 200 % (up to 30 A). Manufacturers' watts-loss figures put a pole at about 2 W at its rating, about 150 mV, so a contact resistance of 10 mΩ is taken (2.25 W at 15 A).

game-design inside manufacturer-style curves for NEC-region residential thermal-magnetic breakers (not IEC 60898): inverse-time thermal trips from a little above the rating (ultimate trip 1.25 ×; a 60 s time constant gives about 30 s at 200 %), and an instantaneous magnetic pickup published as a band near ten times the rating (8 to 12 ×, drawn per breaker). The fictional datasheet's band, tested: 135 %: 30 s to 1 h; 200 %: 10 s to 2 min; 500 %: 1 to 15 s; 13 × and above: within 1 ms.
game-design: a single-pole breaker on a 40 × 90 mm base, 70 mm tall, with the line terminal at the top and the load terminal at the bottom; standalone (no panel until P4); not modelled on a product.

The load (wire) screw terminal of 15 A single-pole plug-on and bolt-on branch breakers, from several makers' public specification sheets and installation instructions, paraphrased (not one vendor's): marked for copper or aluminium (CU/AL), 14 to 10 AWG (some to 8), solid or stranded, with a marked tightening torque of about 4.0 N·m (35 lb·in) for 14 to 10 AWG. The torque is the fictional breaker's marking; NFPA 70-2023 Art. 110.14(D) requires the marked value (cited by number). No UL 486A-B torque table is used.

game-design: a panelboard branch breaker's line side is a stab or bolt onto the panel's bus, not a wire screw. Standing alone on its base (and on a DIN rail, D12), this breaker's line side takes a wire, so its line screw stands in for the bus connection, as the utility service stands in for the load centre; it copies the load terminal's values (14 to 10 AWG CU/AL, solid or stranded, 4.0 N·m). P4's panel replaces it with the bus.

game-design: the fictional breaker is marked for one conductor per terminal (some makers list two of 14 to 10 AWG); two physically fit under the clamp, and a second makes a worse termination (D8). The 13 ± 2 mm strip length is chosen to fill the clamp without exposed copper; it is not a published figure.
game-design: conductors enter the line terminal from the top face and the load terminal from the bottom face of the 90 mm tall base, leaving along ±y; not modelled on a product.

game-design: the breaker's base clips onto a 35 mm DIN rail (IEC 60715) and takes its full 40 mm base width along the rail (D12's demo puts it on a DIN mount). A real one-pole DIN-rail breaker is one module, about 17.5 to 18 mm wide; the base's width is kept so the entry's size is unchanged. Its terminals follow the panelboard branch-breaker class (a CU/AL load screw at 4.0 N·m), not the DIN-rail (UL 489 box-terminal) class. A real DIN-rail breaker is one module of about 18 mm per pole; a future entry version may take that.

game-design: a slotted and square (Robertson) combination head, as on many North American branch-breaker and panel screws (common practice, not one product); the drive type is a name and its size is not modelled.

NBS Building Science Series 103 (W. J. Meese and R. W. Beausoliel, 1977; read in the P3 source pre-audit, ADR 0018 §4.1): good branch-circuit screw-terminal connections dropped 3 to 8 mV at 15 A, 0.2 to 0.5 mΩ. The class value 0.3 mΩ is taken as R₀, the contact resistance at the marked torque with a copper conductor at 20 °C; the engine scales it for torque, strip length, conductor count, strand spread, nicks, crimps and aluminium (ADR 0018 §4).

game-design calibration (ADR 0018 §3.3, §11), for F3.6's hot-spot node: the heat path into the device, 0.026 W/K, is calibrated, not measured: with 14 AWG copper at 15 A it puts BSS 103's 18 to 36 W glowing connections between the threshold of visible glow (the Draper point, about 525 °C) and about 1000 °C. The clamp's heat capacity, 1.1 J/K, is a physics estimate: about 3 g of brass clamp parts × about 380 J/(kg·K).

game-design: the fictional breaker's wire screws clamp the conductor under a pressure plate (a saddle) rather than wrapping it under a binding head, so bare strands are held (ADR 0018 §4.3); the plate grips 10 mm of conductor, inside the 13 ± 2 mm strip. Not modelled on a product.
